title: Stop Planning For The Year You Think You're Going To Have - Life Science Leader
description:
That lesson has direct implications for annual planning.
Make The Assumptions Visible Traditional annual planning often hides assumptions inside the numbers.
Define the most likely alternatives and determine which parts of the strategy change, and which do not.
Separate Commitments From Choices Scenario planning does not mean creating five elaborate versions of the annual operating plan.
Annual planning can often create a false sense of certainty.
text:
By Jason C. Bork

Years ago, a mentor recommended Clayton Christensen’s How Will You Measure Your Life? One story from the book has stayed with me.

When Honda entered the U.S. motorcycle market, its deliberate strategy was to compete in the market Harley-Davidson dominated. Honda had a strategy, invested behind it, and began executing.

But things didn’t go according to plan. Americans liked their Harleys.

Meanwhile, Honda employees were using the company’s much smaller Super Cub motorcycles around Los Angeles, including recreationally. People noticed. They started asking where they could buy them.

An opportunity emerged that wasn’t a part of Honda’s original strategy.

Eventually, Honda shifted resources toward the smaller motorcycles. What began as an unexpected opportunity became an important part of its U.S. strategy.

Christensen uses the story to distinguish between deliberate strategy, the strategy we intentionally set out to execute, and emergent strategy, which develops as new information, problems, and/or opportunities appear.

The lesson isn’t to avoid having a strategy.

It is to have a strategy while remaining open to evidence that the strategy needs to change.

That lesson has direct implications for annual planning.

Every year, leadership teams spend significant time developing revenue forecasts, allocating budgets, prioritizing programs, setting milestones, and approving headcount.

Then the year starts.

In life sciences, reality has a habit of rewriting the plan.

A clinical trial reads out differently than expected. The FDA provides new feedback. Funding takes longer to secure. A competitor publishes unexpected data. A partnership emerges. A specific technology matures faster than anticipated. A portfolio decision redirects resources almost overnight.

The problem isn’t that organizations are planning too much.

It is that too many organizations plan as though one version of the future is going to happen…and then stay committed to that plan in the face of growing evidence that their assumptions, which were foundational to their strategy, no longer hold true.

The better approach is to build plans and processes designed for uncertainty.

Plan For Multiple Futures

I experienced this firsthand during my career at Eli Lilly.

At the time, Lilly was facing several major patent expirations. We did not know exactly what the future organization would look like. Would Lilly remain a fully integrated pharmaceutical company (FIPCO) owning nearly all aspects of the discovery and development engine? Would it rely more heavily on outside development partners and merely coordinate asset development among disparate service providers? Would new therapeutic innovations primarily be in-licensed or acquired instead of internally developed, changing how the company operated?

Those different futures would have a major impact on how we shaped and evolved our Project Leadership and Project Management organization.

So rather than planning against a single future, we explored several.

First, we described multiple plausible future states in enough detail to understand which competencies would matter most and how our organization would need to deliver.

Next, we identified what would have to happen for each future to become reality. What internal decisions, external developments, or other factors would move us in that direction? When were those events likely to occur? We completed that work across several scenarios.

Then we looked for what those possible futures had in common.

Which organizational strategies made sense across the most likely possible futures? Those were areas where we could invest and move aggressively now.

Which strategies depended heavily on a particular future? For those, we identified when we expected to know more and what information would allow us to make a better decision.

That distinction was powerful.

If an activity was necessary under almost every plausible scenario, we didn’t need to wait for perfect information. We could move forward confidently.

If a decision depended on a particular outcome, we could identify the decision point, determine what information was missing, and establish when that information was expected to become available. Then we either waited for the ‘trigger’ or made a decision at-risk, fully comprehending the intended and unintended consequences of the timing of that decision.

Instead of saying:

“We don’t know yet, so we can’t plan.”

We could say:

“This is how we will move forward now. This is what depends on a future outcome that may be within or outside of our control, and the information it will deliver. And these are the anticipated directions we could go in when we make that decision.”

That creates a very different organization. Uncertainty stops being a reason for paralysis and becomes something that can be managed.

Make The Assumptions Visible

Traditional annual planning often hides assumptions inside the numbers.

They shouldn’t be hidden.

For every major strategic initiative, leadership teams should ask three questions:

What has to be true?

Identify the assumptions supporting the strategy, including scientific, financial, regulatory, commercial, operational and organizational assumptions.

When will we know?

Determine when important information will become available and establish explicit decision points.

What will we do if the answer is different?

Define the most likely alternatives and determine which parts of the strategy change, and which do not.

This turns an annual plan from a forecast into a decision architecture.

Separate Commitments From Choices

Scenario planning does not mean creating five elaborate versions of the annual operating plan. Most organizations don’t need five plans. They need one strategy with clearly defined branches.

Think of it as a tree.

The trunk represents actions that make sense across most scenarios. Those should be executed firmly and efficiently.

The branches represent decisions that depend on future information. Those should have defined assumptions, triggers, decision dates and potential actions.

This distinction helps prevent a common problem: delaying everything because one part of the future is uncertain.

If 70% of the work makes sense across three plausible scenarios, there is little reason to wait on that 70%. Move forward while maintaining flexibility around the remaining decisions.

Strategy Needs A Plan And Permission To Evolve

Honda did not abandon strategy. It responded when reality provided new information. Our organizations should do the same, especially in today’s environment, where technology and change have an increasingly rapid impact on our future.

Annual planning can often create a false sense of certainty. Once the budget is approved, objectives are documented and milestones are entered into the system, leaders can become psychologically invested in making reality match the plan.

But the purpose of a plan is not to predict the future correctly. “All models are wrong, but some are useful,” wrote the statistician George E.P. Box.

It requires leadership to maintain a big picture focus and understanding of external shifts within the market or ecosystem — when is our annual plan no longer useful?

The purpose is to prepare the organization to make better decisions as the future becomes clearer.

A strong annual plan makes clear:

what the organization believes;

what it does not yet know;

what it will do regardless;

what information could change its direction; and

when critical decisions need to be made.

Uncertainty and change are far less disruptive when employees understand the assumptions behind the strategy, and the different directions the organization may take. When a change comes, the reaction should not be, “Where did this come from?”

It should be: “Oh, yes. We knew this was one of the possibilities. Glad we planned for it.”

Don’t plan for the year you think you’re going to have. Build a plan for the decisions you’re going to have to make.

About The Author:

Jason C. Bork is President and Founder at Pintail Solutions, a life sciences consultancy. He is a seasoned life science executive with more than 30 years of experience across large pharma, CRO, and start-up organizations. He is an entrepreneur known for seeing the essence, distilling the complex into actionable steps, and developing those around him to new levels of fulfillment. From business strategy, organizational change, and operational excellence, Jason enables organizations to solve critical challenges, deliver high-impact projects, and move into the future with clarity and confidence.

title: Delta Reports Record Revenue But Cuts Profit Forecast, Putting United's Next Results In Focus
description:

Its refinery still contributed a 13-cent-per-gallon benefit to the adjusted fuel price.
It expects an additional $6 billion in fuel costs this year.
Delta’s results illustrate that rather clearly.
They also show how quickly higher costs can consume the benefit of higher fares and (thankfully) suggest there is a ceiling as to how high carriers can raise fares.
text:
Delta Air Lines reported record third-quarter revenue this morning, but sharply lowered its full-year profit forecast as higher fuel costs continued to eat into its earnings. Passengers are still paying more to fly, especially up front…but even Delta cannot charge enough to escape the consequences of expensive fuel.

Delta’s Quarterly Results Show Strong Demand, But Fuel Is Eating Into Profits

Delta’s September-quarter results offer a useful look at the airline industry right now: strong revenue, resilient premium demand, and considerable pressure on costs.

Here are some of the key numbers:

Metric Third Quarter 2026 Year-Over-Year Change Adjusted revenue $17.6 billion Up 16% Adjusted pre-tax profit $1.5 billion Up 1% Adjusted operating margin 9.4% Down from 11.1% Adjusted earnings per share $1.72 Up from $1.70 Adjusted fuel expense $4.1 billion Up 62%

These are adjusted figures, which exclude third-party refinery sales and certain other items. Delta’s reported revenue was $20.2 billion. Its refinery still contributed a 13-cent-per-gallon benefit to the adjusted fuel price.

Delta now expects full-year adjusted earnings of $5.10 to $5.60 per share, versus its previous forecast of $6.50 to $7.50. It expects an additional $6 billion in fuel costs this year.

Delta’s Premium Strategy Is Working, But Still A Work In Progress

Premium revenue grew 18% on a 6% increase in premium seats, showing that Delta is not only putting more expensive seats on its aircraft, it is finding passengers willing to fill them and pay more.

That supports the approach Delta has taken for years. Give travelers a reason to choose your airline, and some will pay a premium to do so. The seat matters, but so do the schedule, service, lounges, and reliability. Delta may not be the “on-time machine” it once was, but still outperforms its peers.

But in a time of war and inflation, record revenue did not translate to record profitability.

Simply put, Delta or any airline can sell more expensive tickets but remain worse off if its costs rise faster. Delta’s results illustrate that rather clearly. And while fuel is the biggest problem, non-fuel costs per unit of capacity also rose 7.3%.

It is too premature to say that Delta is struggling or conversely to say that its premium strategy has made it immune to the problems facing everyone else. It remains profitable, but its margins have narrowed.

Delta expects approximately 20% revenue growth in the fourth quarter. Airlines will continue trying to recover their higher costs from travelers for as long as travelers keep paying and with schedules pared back this autumn and the loss of Spirit, I expect much higher holiday fares than last year.

Will United Tell A Similar Story On October 20?

United will report its results after the market closes on October 20, followed by its earnings call the next morning.

My expectation is that we will hear a similar broad story: strong demand, particularly for premium travel, accompanied by an expensive fuel bill. In July, United expected to recover 80% to 90% of its increased fuel costs through revenue in the third quarter and all of the increase in the fourth. I will be particularly interested in whether it still believes that is achievable or it has been forced to moderate fare hikes due to competitive pressures.

United is pursuing a more ambitious expansion, and I admire that. More destinations and a better onboard product give travelers reasons to choose it. They also require substantial investment, whereas Delta has taken a much more cautious approach toward growth.

Obviously, the only useful comparison in terms of this “battle” will be how much profit each airline keeps from the revenue it generates. A larger route map is exciting, but a larger route map that produces stronger margins is much more impressive for shareholders and longterm sustainability.

And neither airline’s third-quarter results will settle the argument over Musk, Starlink, or status matches. That controversy developed near the end of the quarter, while the latest offers came afterward. I would not turn these earnings into a referendum on a few days of angry tweets.

> Read More: Delta CEO Denies Rejecting Starlink Over Elon Musk, Says “I Drive A Tesla”

CONCLUSION

Delta’s results suggest passengers still want to travel and remain willing to pay for a better experience. They also show how quickly higher costs can consume the benefit of higher fares and (thankfully) suggest there is a ceiling as to how high carriers can raise fares.

I expect United to report strong demand too. What remains to be seen is whether it can turn that demand into better margins or will have to trim its own expectations. Delta has given us the first substantial look at the quarter…United will give us a much more useful comparison on October 20.

text:
Dr. Ali Karatay's coffee-painted portrait of Pope Francis highlights art's power to connect cultures and celebrate shared humanity.

WOODLAND, Calif., Oct. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A portrait of Pope Francis created with coffee by artist Dr. Ali Karatay, founder and CEO of Erguvan Art & Academy, was presented to the Pope at the Vatican. Inspired by love, peace, and shared human values, the artwork reflects Karatay's belief in art as a universal language that connects people across cultures and beliefs.

More Than an Artistic Medium: Coffee

For Dr. Karatay, choosing coffee was an essential part of the artwork's message.

Enjoyed in countless ways around the world, coffee celebrates cultural diversity while bringing people together. Beyond its flavors and aromas, it represents conversation, hospitality, friendship, and connection. Across generations and traditions, the simple act of sharing coffee has long offered opportunities for people to meet, exchange stories, and discover common ground.

Through coffee's natural tones, Karatay transforms this familiar experience into a visual expression of unity.

"Art is one of the most powerful languages we share as human beings. A color, a line, a brushstroke, or even a familiar taste or scent can create a meaningful connection between people. I believe art has the power to move beyond what divides us and reveal the humanity we share," says Dr. Karatay.

A Meaningful Response from the Vatican

The portrait was sent to the Vatican in December 2021, accompanied by a personal letter explaining its inspiration. In an official response dated June 20, 2022, the Pope's Private Secretariat confirmed that the artwork had been presented to Pope Francis. The letter also conveyed appreciation for the artistic technique, effort, and meaning behind the portrait.

Erguvan Art & Academy: An International Art Movement

Founded by Dr. Karatay, Erguvan Art & Academy is an international youth art movement dedicated to creativity, education, and collaboration. Through more than 30 projects and initiatives, Erguvan brings together artists and art enthusiasts from around the world.

In August 2026, Erguvan opened its first physical art center in Woodland, California, creating a new space for artistic expression, learning, and collaboration.

Guided by its motto, "Art Will Save the World," Erguvan continues to explore art's potential to inspire connection, healing, and peace.

Dr. Karatay's coffee-painted portrait embodies this vision, showing how a simple medium can carry a message beyond cultural boundaries.

text:
Greta Garbo, lauded actor of Hollywood’s silent and Golden Era, stars in a new, highly unexpected role: the spokesperson for a cutting-edge initiative from global manufacturer SKF to change how the world pays for energy-saving technology.

In 1921, Garbo starred in one of SKF’s earliest promotional films, so consider this return a full-circle reunion of sorts. Now, the actress (or her AI form, at least) returns to the helm of the “Pay Like It’s 1919” campaign, which represents the fusion of SKF’s practical application of AI technology with a modern and undoubtedly attention-grabbing approach that’s a nod to the company’s 119-year-old legacy.

Of course, a lot has changed since then: Cars are now computers with wheels, and humans have landed on the moon not once, but six times. For SKF, though, the importance of pursuing more sustainable and efficient energy utilization — and making the means to do so accessible — has remained unchanged, a North Star for the future of energy. But don’t assume “pay like it’s 1919” means SKF is accepting vintage bills and cents, requiring a quick sprint to an antique store. They’re not bringing back the currency of yore… Well, at least not in the way you might be imagining. In 1919, SKF let companies pay with their energy savings — and they want to do it again.

“We may offer performance-based payment structures linked to energy savings, allowing parts of the investment to be paid over time,” says Annika Ölme, chief technology officer at SKF, of the initiative. “Each arrangement is assessed individually. The aim is to make energy-efficient technology easier to put to work.” In a campaign video, an AI-generated Garbo reiterates this logic plainly: “New inventions need new ways to reach the many.” (Garbo’s family and estate, Harriet Brown & Company Inc., were closely involved in the campaign’s development and approval of her portrayal, per SKF.)

SKF is a trailblazer in zero-friction manufacturing via its magnetic bearings technology, a method of eliminating friction from inside the machinery. In the industrial sector, friction looks like misaligned machinery or poorly lubricated mechanisms, and it’s estimated that 20 percent of the world’s energy is wasted overcoming friction in the manufacturing process. Observing the magnetic bearings, one might think it’s magic, but in layman’s terms, it simply relies on magnetic polarity to avoid mechanical contact between the rotating and stationary bearings. The shaft levitates within the bearing as it rotates at upwards of 80,000 revolutions per minute (RPM).

For manufacturers utilizing these bearings, the benefits of zero-friction technology may look like lower energy consumption, reduced maintenance requirements (magnetic bearings don’t require oil lubricants, nor do they experience wear), or a reduced carbon footprint. Harkening back to SKF’s commitment to sustainability, that reduced carbon footprint has become an entry point for any manufacturer considering integrating this technology — and “Pay Like It’s 1919” is an extra insurance policy to ensure the barrier to entry is lower than what is most often seen in the magnetic bearings industry.

“With ‘Pay Like It’s 1919,’ we are addressing the investment barrier,” Ölme says. “Our Fighting Friction initiatives extend that thinking to the barriers that prevent good ideas from making a difference. The ambition is consistent: help innovation reach the point where it creates value for industry and society.”

title: Fired OpenAI employees question the company's commitment to safety - NPR
description:
It said the employees were fired for mishandling sensitive information and said the company has not abandoned its safety commitment.
The three employees dismissed by OpenAI last week worked on teams that focus on AI safety and making the company's models follow human intentions and values.
OpenAI allowed researchers from METR and Redwood Research, another AI safety research organization, to examine internal records related to the Hugging Face hack.
A second fired OpenAI employee, Korbak, was the technical point of contact for the METR/Redwood Research investigation.
In a statement to NPR, METR declined to comment on the OpenAI employees' firings.
text:
Three former OpenAI employees are raising concerns over the circumstances of their dismissals and the company's commitment to safety, amid intense public scrutiny of the artificial intelligence industry's ability to responsibly develop the technology.

The former employees, Mikita Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, alleged that OpenAI fired them last week over pretexts and punished them for either being outspoken about safety or working with outside researchers. They also expressed worries the company may walk back a recent safety commitment.

OpenAI has repeatedly denied the allegations. It said the employees were fired for mishandling sensitive information and said the company has not abandoned its safety commitment.

The dispute comes at a fraught time for the AI industry and OpenAI in particular. Over the summer, OpenAI's agents hacked into companies, communicated with each other without authorization and attempted to cover their tracks. Unlike chatbots, agents are AI systems that can carry out tasks autonomously for an extended period of time.

The most serious hack, of software company Hugging Face, contributed to the resignation of a researcher at rival Anthropic who issued dire warnings about the trajectory of the technology. The resignation captured the attention of figures outside of the AI field including lawmakers. Many, including some executives of the top AI companies, have called for various ways to avert disaster, including slowing down the development of the most advanced AI.

In the meanwhile, OpenAI has been reviewing its agents' activities in recent months and notifying organizations whose digital infrastructure has been affected.

As a response to the safety concerns, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on Sep. 12 that the company will follow its rival Anthropic in expanding access to third-party evaluators, who assess the safety of AI systems and the practices of developers.

The three employees dismissed by OpenAI last week worked on teams that focus on AI safety and making the company's models follow human intentions and values. Two of them were involved in investigating the Hugging Face hack.

In a letter to OpenAI's safety leadership that the fired employees posted on X this week, they urged the company to stay committed to working with third-party researchers, to preserve human's ability to monitor model behavior and to "continue to support an open and transparent culture of dialogue" between in-house safety researchers and external ones. They also warned their firings were having a chilling effect on their former OpenAI colleagues.

In a statement OpenAI posted on X, the company said it is still committed to bringing in third-party evaluators and that it agreed with the fired employees's recommendations. The company said the three were fired last week because they "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information."

The former employees have disputed OpenAI's explanation of their firings. None of them responded to NPR's interview requests.

"In the exit call, I was told OpenAI no longer trusts me because I was speaking too much to third party safety organizations, implying I leaked company [intellectual property]. I never shared company IP," Balesni wrote on X on Thursday. He said he was involved in investigating the OpenAI agents' hack on Hugging Face.

"If OpenAI has specific concerns, I invite them to write to us directly. I expect they will not, because our firing was pretextual," Balesni continued.

He said he worried that OpenAI will use the firings as an excuse to cut off its relationship with Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), a nonprofit that focuses on evaluating risks of humans losing control of AI. OpenAI allowed researchers from METR and Redwood Research, another AI safety research organization, to examine internal records related to the Hugging Face hack.

A second fired OpenAI employee, Korbak, was the technical point of contact for the METR/Redwood Research investigation. "I was told verbally I was fired because of the way I communicated with METR. No details on what I said or did or when. No other reasons were given and nothing was put in writing," Korbak wrote on X, echoing Balesni's concerns.

The report produced by METR and Redwood Research in the wake of the Hugging Face hack shed light on the scale of the attack as well as the degree to which the agents acted in undesirable ways. The authors of the report called the investigation "brief" and many in the AI safety field have called for expanded access to independent evaluators at AI companies to make sure they investigate similar incidents or other safety concerns thoroughly.

In a statement to NPR, METR declined to comment on the OpenAI employees' firings.

Wang, the third OpenAI employee fired last week, coined the word "pacing," which describes a way of slowing down development of the most advanced AI systems so that safety can catch up, according to the letter she and her two colleagues sent to OpenAI's safety leadership. The term was invoked in an open letter calling for such a slowdown signed by over a thousand staff members from top AI companies in July, after the Hugging Face hack.

Wang wrote on X that she was fired over accessing an executive's email. But she said she had access to the inbox for work reasons in the past and wasn't able to get IT to remove the access once she no longer needed it.

"The reasons that we were provided for our terminations are simply not adding up. We're hearing people are now being told vague rumors internally to discredit us," Wang wrote. "The message to everyone still at OpenAI is clear: raise concerns or work closely with outside safety groups, and you could be next, without being told why."

OpenAI said in a statement to NPR that the three terminated employees violated policies more than once, and the mishandling of information went beyond their work with an outside evaluation group.

OpenAI also shared an internal memo from an unnamed research leader that it said was shared with the company on Wednesday, before the three ex-employees took to social media.

In the memo, the research leader said the company "strongly" agreed with the three ex-employees' recommendations. "We do not terminate employees for raising concerns," the leader wrote.

"OpenAI leadership is saying they strongly agree with our letter. Let's see how that pans out," Wang wrote on X.

text:
The United States has expanded its crackdown on foreign-worker hiring by suspending several major Indian IT companies from the employment-based Green Card sponsorship process, citing alleged fraud and concerns that foreign workers are displacing American employees.

US Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling announced the suspension of major outsourcing firms, including Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini, from the Permanent Labor Certification Programme, commonly known as PERM.

“I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labor Certification Program some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world — Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini,” Sonderling said.

The move could affect Indian professionals seeking permanent residency through employer sponsorship, particularly those whose applications have not yet reached the labour certification stage. The suspension prevents affected companies from filing new PERM applications while the restrictions remain in force.

The US administration has alleged that some employers misused foreign-worker programmes through fraudulent filings, wage undercutting and practices that disadvantaged American workers. Sonderling said the government intended to prioritise domestic employment.

PERM is a key step in the employment-based Green Card process. Employers generally must obtain labour certification from the US Department of Labor before proceeding with sponsorship for permanent residency. The process includes wage assessments and recruitment requirements intended to protect US workers.

The action comes amid heightened scrutiny of the H-1B visa system and employment-based immigration under President Donald Trump. Indian professionals are particularly exposed to potential delays because of longstanding Green Card backlogs for applicants from India.

For affected workers, the immediate impact could include delayed applications and uncertainty over immigration timelines. Employees approaching the six-year H-1B limit may face additional complications, although eligibility for extensions depends on individual circumstances and applicable immigration rules.

The full impact will depend on the scope and duration of the suspensions and how US authorities implement the measures.

text:
The consumer goods industry had another busy few weeks for personnel shifts. Hiring announcements from companies such as Molson Coors, Keurig Dr Pepper, the Coca-Cola Co., and others provide a glimpse into massive shifts happening at the executive leadership level.

Across these leadership moves, top CPG companies are prioritizing seasoned executives who can drive digital transformations, integrate AI planning tools and navigate complex corporate restructures or M&A integrations. Rather than focusing solely on traditional operational management, these new hires are tasked with executing granular, data-enabled pricing and supply chain strategies to combat consumer price sensitivity and unlock scalable growth.

Here's a look at the recent leadership announcements and what they mean for the industry.

Catalina Snacks

Catalina Snacks, a maker of better-for-you cereals and snacks, has appointed Charlotte Mostaed as chief marketing officer to lead the brand's marketing strategy and drive commercial expansion. In this role, Mostaed will oversee creative strategy, brand positioning, consumer insights, e-commerce and retail initiatives to widen Catalina’s market reach and deepen consumer engagement as the company continues to scale.

Mostaed joins Catalina from Health-Ade Kombucha, where she served as CMO and built a growth model that doubled the business' revenue, expanded household penetration to millions of new consumers, and helped position the company for acquisition. Her earlier background includes senior marketing roles at POM Wonderful and Procter & Gamble.

According to Catalina CEO Doug Behrens, Mostaed’s proven track record of turning consumer insights into brand momentum will be instrumental as the company expands its portfolio beyond 30,000 retail locations nationwide.

Molson Coors

Molson Coors Beverage Co. has appointed 27-year company veteran Matthew Hook to lead its Americas supply chain operations starting Oct. 12, succeeding longtime executive Brian Erhardt.

Hook, who most recently served as VP of manufacturing operations for North America, brings end-to-end operational expertise across 11 regional breweries and packaging facilities. His past contributions include modernizing brewery infrastructure, driving digital supply chain transformations, optimizing Canadian distribution networks and streamlining integrated business planning.

The appointment comes as new president and CEO Rahul Goyal drives a broader organizational transition toward a leaner business model backed by ERP and AI technology investments. Goyal’s strategy focuses on strengthening core and economy beer brands, scaling non-alcoholic offerings, improving distribution for Coors Light and revitalizing Miller Lite through localized promotional execution.

According to leadership, Hook’s comprehensive systemic perspective across geographies will support the company’s efforts to upgrade its supply chain and commercial technology capabilities.

Keurig Dr Pepper & Kimberly Clark

Keurig Dr Pepper and Kimberly-Clark are finalizing executive leadership teams in preparation for major corporate restructures and transactions. KDP has appointed Russ Torres as CEO of Global Coffee Co. effective Nov. 3, ahead of the company's planned split into two standalone businesses in early 2027.

Torres, who brings 30 years of CPG experience from roles at Kimberly-Clark, Newell Brands, and Mondelez, will report to KDP CEO Tim Cofer and oversee the integration of KDP and JDE Peet's coffee operations into an entity expected to generate $16 billion in annual revenue across more than 100 markets.

Concurrently, Kimberly-Clark is reshaping its leadership structure as it prepares to complete its acquisition of Kenvue in late 2026. Following Torres' departure from his integration role, chief strategy officer Jeff Melucci will oversee integration planning while CFO Nelson Urdaneta leads synergy delivery. The company also appointed Kenvue’s Carlos De Jesus to lead the post-merger North America segment and manage the growth organization.

Coca-Cola & Colgate-Palmolive

Coca‑Cola and Colgate-Palmolive have appointed new commercial and customer development leaders to steer retail strategy and navigate shifting consumer demands.

At Coca-Cola, Roberto Mercadé will become chief customer and commercial officer on Nov. 1, succeeding Jorge Garduño and reporting to global CMO and chief customer commercial officer Manolo Arroyo. Mercadé, a 34-year company veteran who most recently led The McDonald’s Division, will be replaced in that role by Pamela Stewart, leaving his former position as chief customer officer of retail open.

Concurrently, Colgate-Palmolive has named former Campbell’s Co. executive Mike Pierson as EVP of customer development for the U.S. market, bringing more than 20 years of CPG sales experience from past roles at PepsiCo, Pepperidge Farm and GoGo squeeZ.

These leadership appointments come as both companies focus on refined revenue growth management and technology integration to combat inflation and price sensitivity. Mercadé will oversee localized price-pack architecture, promotional trade spend and margin alignment across retail and foodservice partners to balance consumer affordability with premiumization initiatives. Meanwhile, Pierson will lead Colgate’s commercial retail relationships, leveraging data-driven strategies and the company’s "Promo AI" tools to optimize promotional structures, address North American price-gap issues and improve trade spend ROI without relying on heavy discounting.

Nissin Foods

Nissin Foods USA, maker of Cup Noodles and Top Ramen, has hired Glenn Lawse as VP of supply chain to strengthen operational capabilities and support long-term growth. Lawse brings over 25 years of global supply chain leadership from companies like Campari Group, Ferrero, and Johnson & Johnson. His track record includes executing large-scale digital transformations, logistics network redesigns and AI-enabled forecasting initiatives that delivered significant inventory reductions, cost savings and operational efficiencies.

Lawse’s appointment comes as Nissin Foods transitions toward a fully integrated, AI-enabled supply chain. The company is modernizing its operations by adopting Highspring’s supply chain-as-a-service platform and Blue Yonder’s planning software to replace legacy systems.

According to President and CEO Yukio Yokoyama, these advanced planning tools will enhance cross-functional visibility and agility, enabling smarter decision-making, faster responses to market shifts and reduced operational costs.

Ocean Spray

Agricultural cooperative Ocean Spray Cranberries has appointed Brad Hartzell as chief supply chain officer and Kevin Zidron as chief strategy and transformation officer. These hires mark the first major executive appointments under Abigail Buckwalter, who became president and CEO in June 2026.

Hartzell, who succeeds retiring 22-year veteran Earl Larson, brings over 25 years of global supply chain experience from KDC/ONE, NovaTaste and International Flavors & Fragrances to manage global logistics across 700 family farms and distribution to over 100 countries.

Zidron, joining from Nestlé Health Science, Vital Proteins and Kraft Heinz, will lead enterprise strategy, transformation, project management and commercial insights to drive long-term business growth. His role aligns with Ocean Spray's recent strategic moves into RTD alcohol partnerships and zero-sugar beverage lines.

According to Buckwalter, the additions of Hartzell and Zidron will enhance the cooperative’s supply chain efficiency and execution discipline as it positions itself for its next growth phase.

What This Means

As consumer goods companies navigate an inflationary environment and rapid tech shifts, these executive moves highlight five major trends reshaping CPG leadership:

Supply Chain as the Strategic Engine: Supply chain roles are no longer focused solely on operational maintenance. Companies are placing supply chain executives at the center of their enterprise strategy. The moves from brands such as Molson Coors, Ocean Spray, Nissin Foods USA and Catalina Snacks show a push to bring in leaders with deep backgrounds in digital supply networks, continuous improvement and operational integration.

Digital Transformation and Embedded AI: Experience guiding organizations through digital shifts is a sought-after skill set. Whether deploying AI-enabled forecasting platforms, migrating away from legacy tools (Nissin Foods), updating ERP systems (Molson Coors) or embedding data-driven trade models like "Promo AI" (Colgate-Palmolive), executives are expected to combine traditional operational oversight with tech-enabled capabilities.

Granular RGM Tactics: Across customer development and marketing roles, companies are moving away from broad actions toward hyper-targeted, surgical execution and targeted pricing. Leaders at Coca-Cola, Colgate-Palmolive and Molson Coors are being tasked with managing price-pack architecture, localized promotional spend and channel strategies to drive growth while navigating consumer price sensitivity.

Large-Scale Transformations and M&A: Several of these announcements highlight a demand for executives who have previously navigated high-stakes corporate restructures, integrations or acquisitions. Examples include Russ Torres stepping in to lead KDP's coffee business separation after leading integration efforts at Kimberly-Clark, executives managing leadership shifts around Kimberly-Clark's pending Kenvue transaction, and previous growth background at brands positioned for acquisition, such as Health-Ade for Catalina's CMO.

Sharing the Institutional Knowledge: There is a clear trend of cross-pollination across major consumer goods players. Enterprises are bringing in leaders with decades of combined experience from top-tier CPG competitors — such as Nestlé, PepsiCo, Kraft Heinz, Procter & Gamble and Campbell's — to shorten learning curves and execute complex business playbooks quickly.

text:
Walmart’s multibillion-dollar push to replace human workers with robots is reportedly hitting snags as the machinery struggles to carry dog food and Thanksgiving turkeys or handle cardboard boxes.

A simple task called “breakpack” – when workers remove items from cardboard boxes to ship out individually – is easy for Walmart’s more than 140,000 warehouse workers, who also unload trucks, operate forklifts, sort and store goods on shelves, and send out shipments.

But it’s a challenge for the new warehouse robots, which are too small to carry and unload the same cardboard boxes, according to a Wall Street Journal report.

It might sound like a simple fix – replace the boxes. And that’s what Walmart is planning to do. But the largest retail chain in the world has been using the same cardboard boxes for more than two decades, urging workers to reuse the boxes to save on costs.

1/1Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE

Now Walmart is planning to throw all those boxes – which cost an average of $1 each – in the trash, replacing them with new ones that are 1 ½ inches shorter and need to be taped closed, a new step that will cost more money, the report said.

Philip McIlrath, the manager of an Indiana apparel warehouse using the new boxes, told the Journal it’s “a small change,” but for workers, “it’s changing their daily routine quite a bit.” He argued the new boxes will eventually reduce stocking time, which will lower labor costs.

Walmart did not immediately respond to The Post’s request for comment.

The small robots, which move on wheels through the warehouses using motion sensors, struggle to hold oversized or heavy items, like turkeys – a problem that emerged a few years ago just ahead of the Thanksgiving rush, the report said.

Workers in a newly-automated grocery warehouse in California noticed that the machine’s robotic arms fumbled large frozen turkeys. It required a shift to nearby grocery warehouses, which helped with turkey shipments to physical stores.

The Brooksville warehouse in Florida, Walmart’s automation test site, is now nearly “fully automated,” according to Rob Montgomery, the head of supply-chain operations at Walmart US overseeing the automation of nearly 200 locations.

About 80% of inventory at Brooksville is moved using automation. But the robotics are still struggling to manage the remaining 20%, which includes heavy objects like large-screen TVs and dog food.

Another issue plaguing the automation rollout is the robots’ finicky tech issues. The bots – made by Symbotic, a Massachusetts robotics company – frequently break down or need maintenance, even from something as minor as dust buildup, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Symbotic said less than 10% of the robots were being fixed at any given time last year, and that percentage has since dropped to about 5%.

“We are kind of in this peak complexity,” Montgomery told the Journal.

In the meantime, automation has driven costs higher, with monthly electric bills at automated grocery facilities reaching $800,000 or more – up from roughly $250,000 a month when operations were mostly manual, the Journal reported, citing an anonymous source.

Walmart expects its spending on automation to peak this year and next, but it also believes the new tech will eventually require fewer warehouse workers, cutting down costs; process more inventory at a faster pace; and limit the frequency of out-of-stock goods.

The company said it will still need human workers for some tasks, like unloading trailers, as well as to work on the robotic systems.

Company executives also said layoffs won’t be necessary because warehouses have such high job turnover.

text:
Nvidia on Thursday scraped together some spare change to commit $1 billion — about 1/60th of its quarterly profits — to funding US scientific discovery over the next five years.

The commitment, announced during an event in Washington, DC, aims to support the research and development of AI — or is it "super intelligence" now? — in fields including quantum computing, healthcare, and energy security.

Nvidia's choice of technologies is not surprising as it has long aspired to fuse AI and high-performance computing. And while LLM training and inference pay Nvidia's bills, the GPU giant has continued to introduce new CUDA libraries specifically for AI-assisted quantum computing, healthcare, drug discovery, and physics simulation.

The initiative is part of the US government's broader Genesis Mission, announced late last year by the Trump administration, which aims to use AI to drive the scientific discoveries necessary to ensure the country's continued technological leadership.

The program marks Nvidia's return to US supercomputing in a big way. The Department of Energy's (DoE) last flagship supercomputers powered by Nvidia, Summitand Sierra, were commissioned all the way back in 2018. The A100-based Perlmutter system launched in 2021 is also notable, but fell far short of the older systems. And while Nvidia never stopped building supers for the US government, they tended to be significantly smaller than the massive AMD-based platforms like Frontier and El Capitan.

That changed last year when Nvidia revealed it would supply the US government with no fewer than seven new supercomputers across the Argonne, Los Alamos, and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratories.

Argonne will house the 100,000 Blackwell-GPU-based Solstice system. Built in collaboration with Oracle, the machine is largely aimed at emerging AI workloads, which don't depend on ultra-high precision computation and instead can get by with 16, eight or even four bits of precision.

That puts Nvidia in a strong position to meet the US government's goals under the Genesis Mission. Over the past few generations of GPUs, Nvidia has traded much of its accelerators' double-precision FP64 grunt in favor of higher throughput at precisions used by more lucrative AI workloads. In the case of its upcoming Vera Rubin platform, Nvidia relies heavily on an FP64 emulation capability based on the Ozaki scheme we looked at in more detail earlier this year.

Los Alamos' upcoming Mission and Vision systems will be powered by these same chips and take advantage of Nvidia's Quantum-X800 InfiniBand.

FP64 emulation comes with compromises, but for workloads that are predominantly AI-optimized and only occasionally need higher precision, it can be worthwhile for the additional matrix FLOPS.

While Nvidia is playing a much bigger role in US scientific computing efforts, it's worth noting that the DoE's biggest super — at least for pure FP64 — will still be powered by AMD. Oak Ridge National Laboratory's Discovery system, which is expected to come online 2029 will be built by HPE's Cray division and feature The House of Zen's FP64-optimized MI430X GPUs and Venice CPUs.

Discovery is expected to offer peak theoretical performance somewhere between 3.3 and 8.5 exaFLOPS depending on whether or not Oak Ridge gets a facility power upgrade.

Dive Brief:

Adidas, H&M Group, Zara-owner Inditex and Danish fashion company Bestseller have launched a coalition that seeks to tackle secondhand textile waste and boost circularity in collaboration with Ghana-based nonprofit The Or Foundation.

The Apparel Recovery Coalition aims to explore how producer responsibility systems — frameworks that entail brands taking responsibility for the lifecycle of their products after consumers are done using them — can boost circular pathways like reuse, recycling and upcycling, as well as support responsible waste management strategies in countries that receive exported secondhand clothing in bulk.

Over the course of its two-year run, ARC plans to develop and test a business model aimed at producer responsibility. The model will be designed to reflect global post-consumer textile flows, and the group also plans to encourage brands, recyclers, sorters, policymakers and affected communities to come up with practical solutions, according to a Sept. 29 press release.

Dive Insight:

The coalition was unveiled last week at Kantamanto Market in Accra, Ghana, which is one of the largest global hubs for sustainable fashion practices like reuse, repair and recycling. The market recirculates around 25 million garments every month, according to an estimate from The Or Foundation. Because of this, the market provides an important lens for understanding post-consumer textiles, in addition to their related environmental and social impacts, like water and soil pollution, the brands said.

One of the stated aims of ARC is to “test more inclusive approaches to governance, design, and implementation” by embedding community perspectives into its project goals, actions, and insights, according to its website.

The coalition, which is also backed by circularity-focused nonprofit Circle Economy, aims to build on the work The Or Foundation has done over the past 15 years to develop Ghana’s existing circular textile ecosystem, the brands said. The nonprofit’s work focuses on the intersection of environmental justice, education and sustainable fashion.

Its first demonstration project will be based in Accra, where the coalition will build on this experience and continue to implement initiatives like infrastructure improvements, environmental remediation and training programs. ARC also said it plans to add another project in a different country that receives large volumes of secondhand clothing.

Adidas, H&M, Inditex and Bestseller will make voluntary financial contributions to support such projects and boost circular economy initiatives, per the release.

“The coalition hopes the evidence and practical learnings generated through these demonstration projects will help inform brands, policymakers, producer responsibility organizations (PROs) and other stakeholders working to strengthen post-consumer textile management systems worldwide,” the release said.

The funding from these fashion brands comes amid growing scrutiny over the environmental footprint incurred through their manufacturing operations and production. Inditex’s latest sustainability report found the company used 705,554 metric tons of raw materials in its products, up from 678,596 metric tons in 2024. Meanwhile, H&M’s most recent sustainability report states the company produced 364,093 metric tons of products in 2025, the equivalent of 36 Eiffel Towers.

text:
For anybody who thought AI companies were about to unlock trillions of dollars in profits, OpenAI has bad news for you: it ain’t happening anytime soon.

Some red-hot reporting from the Financial Times just revealed that OpenAI’s annualized revenue — an estimated guess at a company’s income for the year — is roughly $20 billion lower than anybody had previously expected, including, it seems, OpenAI itself.

Because OpenAI is a private company, it’s important to note that we don’t know for sure what’s going on under the hood. That said, the FT based its reporting on internal memos to investors issued in late September. Basically, the AI lab told backers to expect revenues approaching $50 billion — far shorter than the explosive $70 billion number reported previously.

Though that $70 billion figure was also based on leaked investor memos, OpenAI wasn’t in any hurry to deny it, digging itself into a $20 billion hole. Given the monumental difference between those two figures, investors across the world of finance are taking it as a sign that demand for AI is much lower than previously thought — a signal with ripple effects that extend far beyond OpenAI.

At the closing bells on Wall Street on Thursday, the tech-heavy Nasdaq index was down a whopping 1.25 percent on the day, while the S&P 500 fell by 0.47 percent.

Particularly hard hit were companies sandwiched in the middle of the AI supply-chain, like the chipmaker Nvidia, which tumbled by nearly 3 percent following the news from the FT.

All of this comes a week after consulting firm Bain and Co issued a gloomy report finding that the global AI industry would have to reach annual revenue of $6 trillion by 2031 to justify the amount of spending on AI data centers — a formidable summit, which is now $20 billion farther after the latest disclosures.

Dive Brief:

MMI said Thursday it raised $125 million in a Series D financing to expand access to its robotic microsurgery system in the U.S. as well as key global markets.

The Symani robotic system is designed for soft tissue open surgery, allowing surgeons to repair tiny structures such as lymphatic vessels and nerves. The robot filters out tremors while translating the surgeon’s hand and wrist motions into robotic movement of its miniaturized instruments.

MMI also plans to use the new funds to generate more clinical evidence for robotic microsurgery, including in the REMIND clinical trial evaluating the robot’s use in people with Alzheimer’s disease.

Dive Insight:

MMI’s Symani system received a de novo classification from the Food and Drug Administration for microsurgery in 2024 and was cleared for use in soft tissue dissection the following year. The robot also has CE mark certification in Europe.

About 3,500 complex microsurgical procedures, such as cancer and trauma-related reconstructive surgeries, have been performed worldwide with Symani, which has an installed base of about 50 systems, the company said.

“We’ve proven there is demand for robotic microsurgery at leading institutions around the world,” MMI CEO Mark Toland said in a statement. “Now, our focus is translating that adoption into scale.”

MMI investor BioStar Capital led the latest financing round, and new investors S3 Ventures, Angelini Ventures and an undisclosed strategic corporate investor participated.

MMI said it plans to invest in areas such as energy instruments and digital surgery capabilities, as well as studies such as REMIND and outcomes data that can expand the applications for Symani.

In the REMIND trial, researchers are investigating the safety and feasibility of using Symani for procedures to restore drainage pathways in the deep cervical lymph nodes of the neck in patients with neurodegenerative disease. The goal is to help clear neurotoxins from the brain thought to contribute to the progression of Alzheimer’s.

The Food and Drug Administration gave MMI the go-ahead this summer to expand enrollment in the study to 15 patients.

The Lodging Lowdown is a series from Hotel Dive highlighting major headlines that hospitality professionals may have missed from the week.

The annual Lodging Conference took place in Phoenix this week, with industry professionals gathering to discuss the top trends in hotel development, investment and more.

Hotel companies shared major announcements during the conference, including Wyndham Hotels & Resorts, which partnered with Travel + Leisure Co. to help the company scale its Sports Illustrated Resorts hotel portfolio. Meanwhile, Hyatt debuted new prototypes for its Hyatt Place and Hyatt Studios brands. Hilton’s newly launched Undergraduate brand also has a new-build prototype underway.

Additionally this week, Hilton named a former Uber executive to its newly created chief technology officer role, and Accor tapped a new leader for luxury development in North America. The appointments followed a slate of notable hospitality executive moves in the third quarter.

Here are some other headlines hoteliers should have on their radars this week:

IHG appoints global sales leader

IHG Hotels & Resorts appointed company veteran Leanne Harwood as senior vice president of global sales, according to a Tuesday news release.

In her new role, Harwood is tasked with leading IHG’s global sales organization, driving strategy, performance and customer engagement across corporate, group and meetings and events segments worldwide, per the release.

Harwood has worked at IHG for more than 20 years, most recently serving as senior vice president and managing director of luxury, lifestyle and managed hotels in the Americas. In that position, she oversaw the operations and performance of IHG’s luxury and lifestyle hotel portfolio across the region.

Spire Hospitality opens Alabama hotel under Series by Marriott

Hotel management company Spire Hospitality has reopened the historic St. James Hotel in Selma, Alabama, under the Series by Marriott collection brand, according to a news release shared with Hotel Dive.

Located in a restored building overlooking the Alabama River, the 55-room boutique hotel features guest rooms with modern amenities such as high-speed Wi-Fi, HDTVs and designated workspaces. The property also has an on-site restaurant, a fitness center and flexible meeting space, per the release.

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Hotel Dive free daily newsletter

The Alabama hotel opening comes after Marriott International launched Series by Marriott in May 2025 and later expanded the brand across U.S. destinations such as Miami Beach, Florida, and Santa Monica, California.

Duetto acquires FLYR Hospitality to accelerate AI capabilities

Cloud-based hotel revenue and profit software provider Duetto has acquired FLYR Hospitality, an automated revenue management and business intelligence provider, according to a Thursday news release. Terms of the deal were not disclosed.

The deal expands Duetto’s Revenue & Profit Operating System to include FLYR’s artificial intelligence-powered revenue strategy platform, per the release, and bolsters Duetto’s existing product suite, which includes tools for revenue management, group business and profit benchmarking, the company said.

“FLYR Hospitality’s pricing science and plain-language BI [business intelligence] are some of the best in the category, and combined with our own ML platform, world class RMS, and HotStats’ data, we can give every hotelier, however sophisticated their team, however complex their portfolio, a genuine path to better performance,” Duetto CEO Alex Zoghlin said in a statement.

The deal follows Duetto’s 2025 acquisition of HotStats, a global financial benchmarking company.

Concord Hospitality expands management portfolio

Raleigh, North Carolina-based Concord Hospitality has added more than 12 hotels and restaurants to its management portfolio across “some of the country’s most dynamic hospitality markets,” including Washington, D.C., New Jersey and North Carolina, according to a news release.

Concord will assume management of boutique hotels One Washington Circle, Tapestry Collection by Hilton, in Washington, D.C., as well as The Satire, Autograph Collection, in Alexandria, Virginia. The company also added two properties in New Jersey, including The Union Hotel Flemington, a Tribute Portfolio Hotel, in Flemington, and The Vintedge in Lyndhurst, per the release.

text:
LONG BEACH, Calif. and BENTONVILLE, Ark., Oct. 9, 2026 — SCAN Health Planopens in a new tab (SCAN), and Walmart Inc. (Nasdaq: WMT) today announced the launch of two co-branded Medicare Advantage (MA) plans: SCAN Walmart Health Advantage (HMO) and SCAN Walmart Medicare Complete Chronic Special Needs Plan (C-SNP). The plans combine comprehensive MA coverage with health and wellness support designed to help older adults navigate their individual health needs with greater support, confidence and convenience.

Both offerings will be available beginning January 1, 2027, to eligible Medicare beneficiaries in six counties in Texas and three counties in Arizona. The plan is expected to be available to more than two million Medicare enrollees.

"Walmart plays an important role in the everyday lives of many older adults, whether they're shopping for groceries, filling prescriptions or looking for products that support their health and wellness," said Zack Myers, national general manager of SCAN Health Plan. "Together, we're offering Medicare Advantage plans that combine strong benefits, personalized support and innovative tools that can help members make choices that support their individual health goals."

At the center of the partnership is a shared commitment to improving older adults’ health and wellbeing by making it easier for members to use their benefits for the things they need every day. That includes nutritious foods and over-the-counter benefits that members can use across Walmart’s broad assortment of affordable groceries, health and wellness products and everyday essentials, with convenient ways to shop and access what they need. Together with Walmart’s pharmacy, vision, and broader health and wellness capabilities, the plans are designed to create a more connected experience and help members get more value from their coverage while making choices that support their health goals.

A unique enabler of the experience is Walmart’s Everyday Health SignalsSM, an AI-powered platform that provides nutrition insights from everyday shopping behaviors for members who opt in. Members who choose to participate will receive tailored food recommendations based on their health goals, preferences, and shopping habits.

“For older adults, the value of a health plan can come down to how easy it is to understand and use the benefits available to them,” said Pravene Nath, M.D., group director for consumer health and data solutions at Walmart U.S. “These plans are designed to help support members and Walmart customers with the everyday decisions that impact health and wellness, from groceries and nutritious foods to prescriptions, vision, and other everyday essentials. Walmart Everyday Health SignalsSM helps enrolled members understand the health impact of these decisions and offers personalized, goal-oriented guidance for healthier eating. Walmart and SCAN are creating a convenient and connected experience that helps members get more value from their coverage and better supports their health throughout the year.”

The organizations’ shared commitment to supporting people with chronic conditions is reflected in the SCAN Walmart Medicare Complete Chronic Special Needs Plan (C-SNP). Designed for Medicare beneficiaries with chronic conditions such as diabetes, congestive heart failure and cardiovascular disease, the plan combines specialized benefits with tailored support to help members manage their health. This plan may be a good option for beneficiaries who qualify for full or partial Medicare and Medicaid benefits.

SCAN Walmart Medicare Complete (HMO C-SNP) benefits include:

Low monthly plan premium.*

$0 copays for primary care provider visits.

$0 copays for Tier 1 and Tier 2 prescription drugs.**

$2,400 annually in FlexEssentials allowance for eligible over-the-counter (OTC) items and healthy foods.*** Quarterly limits may apply within the overall annual allowance.

Up to $350 vision allowance.

Comprehensive dental coverage between $3,000 to $4,000.

In addition to the C-SNP product, the partners are also introducing a general enrollment Medicare Advantage HMO product. Members enrolled in the SCAN Walmart Health Advantage (HMO) will have benefits that include:

$0 monthly plan premium.

$0 copays for primary care provider visits.

$0 copays for Tier 1 and Tier 2 prescription drugs**.

Up to $780 annually in FlexEssentials allowance for eligible over-the-counter (OTC) items and healthy foods***. Quarterly limits may apply within the overall annual allowance.

Up to $350 vision allowance.

Comprehensive dental coverage between $3,000 to $3,500.

Access to low-cost prescriptions through Walmart’s Preferred pharmacy.

By combining trusted MA coverage and enhanced resources for people with chronic conditions with the personalized wellness support that Walmart Everyday Health SignalsSM provides, SCAN and Walmart aim to help members understand and use their benefits while making informed choices that support their health every day.

SCAN Walmart Health Advantage (HMO) and SCAN Walmart Medicare Complete (C-SNP) are available in Texas’ Bexar, Chambers, Fort Bend, Harris, Liberty and Montgomery counties and Arizona’s Maricopa, Pima and Pinal counties.

Medicare beneficiaries can enroll in SCAN Walmart Health Advantage (HMO) and SCAN Walmart Medicare Complete (C-SNP) during the Medicare Annual Enrollment Period, October 15 through December 7, for coverage beginning January 1, 2027.

Eligible individuals may have opportunities to enroll in a Walmart C-SNP outside of the Annual Enrollment Period through applicable Special Enrollment Periods.

For more information on the plan and the SCAN and Walmart partnership, please visit www.scandifference.com/walmart

Other providers and pharmacies are available in SCAN Health Plan’s network.

SCAN Health Plan is an HMO plan with a Medicare contract. Enrollment in SCAN Health Plan depends on contract renewal.

* The Chronic Special Needs Plan is only $0 for those that have full Low Income Subsidy (LIS). The premiums for Walmart CSNPs are $16.80 in Arizona and $6.30 in Texas.

** Prescription copayment/coinsurance may vary by plan, county, pharmacy, type, day supply, Part D benefit phase, or for members who receive “Extra Help.

text:
The Japanese apparel group Fast Retailing, owner of the Uniqlo chain, continues to grow at a rapid pace and could finish 2026 as the world’s second-largest fashion retailer. On Thursday, the company reported record annual results, with double-digit increases in both revenue and profit.

The company, whose strength lies in basic wardrobe staples, closed its 2025-26 fiscal year, which ended in August, with revenue of 3.96 trillion yen. At current exchange rates, that is equivalent to roughly $25.6 billion, up 16.6% from the previous year and a new all-time high. Growth accelerated in the second half of the fiscal year, from March to August, when revenue rose 18.8%.

Those growth rates are more than double Inditex’s current pace. The Spanish fashion giant — which includes brands such as Zara and Oysho — reported a 7.6% increase in revenue in its first fiscal half, from February to July.

Net profit attributable to Fast Retailing also surged, rising 25% to around $3.4 billion at current exchange rates.

However, Fast Retailing’s annual sales and profits are remarkably close to what Inditex generated in just six months: €19.8 billion ($22.6 billion) in revenue and €3.0 billion ($3.4 billion) in net profit, respectively.

The Japanese group has also benefited not only from organic sales growth and international expansion, but from a positive currency effect of 4.4% on annual revenue. This is largely due to the current weakness of the yen against currencies such as the euro and China’s renminbi. When sales generated in those markets are converted back into yen, their value in the Japanese currency increases compared with a year earlier. In the case of the euro, for instance, the foreign-exchange benefit is close to 12%.

For Inditex, the effect is the opposite. The company is currently facing a negative currency impact of around 1%, as revenues earned in weaker currencies lose value when translated into the euro, the currency in which the group reports its results.

Becoming No. 1

In any case, the revenue levels reached by Fast Retailing in the past fiscal year have put the company in a position to overtake H&M as Inditex’s closest challenger in global fashion retail, both online and in stores.

The Swedish group’s fiscal year ends on November 30. Through the first nine months of the year, its cumulative sales were down 4.4% from the same period a year earlier. To match Fast Retailing’s revenue in euro terms, H&M would need to post sales growth of nearly 10% in the final stretch of its fiscal year.

However, the owner of Uniqlo is determined to go even further. The company’s chairman, president and CEO, Tadashi Yanai, who is also its largest shareholder with an 18% stake, has set his sights on becoming the world’s leading apparel retailer.

“The goal of becoming global No. 1 has been clear since our founding,” Yanai said in a presentation posted Thursday on Fast Retailing’s investor website. According to the document, that ambition is now “entering a new phase.”

As key drivers of future growth, Yanai points to the potential of Southeast Asia, where Uniqlo aims to become the brand of choice for the region’s young middle class, as well as a major push for GU, Fast Retailing’s value-fashion chain, which currently operates nearly 500 stores in Japan alone.

The presentation suggests that GU may soon accelerate its international expansion. Yanai says the brand’s goal is to become “a global brand” once it completes the ongoing overhaul of its image and commercial strategy, which is being repositioned with a stronger focus on fashion.

In comments reported by Reuters on Thursday, Yanai reiterated a goal he first announced three years ago: turning Fast Retailing into a company with 10 trillion yen in annual revenue, equivalent to roughly €56.5 billion ($64.5 billion) at current exchange rates.

To get there, he aims to add 500 billion yen in revenue each year, or about €2.8 billion ($3.2 billion). At its current scale, it would take the company around 12 years to reach that target.

“When you say 500 billion yen, in our clothing retail sector, ​that’s a massive company," Yanai said. “If you look around the world, there are regions everywhere with that sort of potential.”

Fast Retailing forecasts revenue growth of 12.3% in fiscal 2027, to 4.45 trillion yen, equivalent to more than €25 billion ($28.5 billion). Even so, that would represent an increase somewhat below the pace Yanai has set as a long-term goal.

The Japanese group expects to maintain double-digit growth in both North America and Europe, where sales rose 35% and 39%, respectively, in the last fiscal year.

Combined, those two markets generated nearly €5 billion ($5.7 billion) in revenue for Uniqlo, surpassing China for the first time despite having around 700 fewer stores there.

The group, which operates seven stores in Spain, ended the year with 3,510 outlets worldwide and plans a net addition of 35 stores during the current fiscal year. According to the information released on Thursday, none of those openings are expected to be in the Spanish market.

text:
Siemens deploys its software portfolio for hydrogen at industrial scale, shaping the future of digitally optimized renewable hydrogen production

Physics-based digital twin and real-time optimization

100 MW facility to produce up to 15,000 tons of renewable hydrogen per year, targeting 110,000 tons of CO₂ reduction per year

Siemens and Portugal-based Galp Energia are collaborating to digitalize GalpH2Park in Sines, Portugal. The plant will be one of Europe's largest renewable hydrogen plants once it starts operating at year-end. For the 100 MW hydrogen facility of the first project phase, Siemens is deploying its software portfolio for the hydrogen industry, enabling smarter operations and optimizing the value of the plant. With this deployment, Galp and Siemens are shaping the future of digitally optimized renewable hydrogen production on an industrial scale.

Digital twin at the heart

Central to the collaboration is Siemens' Hydrogen Performance Suite (HPS) – an advanced digital cockpit designed to continuously enhance renewable hydrogen plant operations. At its core lies a predictive Digital Process Twin: a high-fidelity model built on physics-based modeling that delivers operational insights via real-time optimization for faster and data-driven decision-making. To power the digital twin, Siemens deploys an integrated software stack for process modelling, data analytics and real-time visualization – translating complex plant data into clear, actionable insights for operators.

By seamlessly integrating the digital twin with live plant data and external sources, such as grid operators and energy markets, the HPS gives Galp’s operators end-to-end visibility of their facility. The result is smarter production scheduling, and optimized energy procurement. Siemens estimates that the HPS can deliver energy savings of up to 15 percent – a significant lever for both cost competitiveness and sustainability.

"GalpH2Park is a lighthouse for Europe's energy transition”, said Axel Lorenz, Executive Vice President Automation Process Industries at Siemens. “We are convinced that digital innovation is the key to making renewable hydrogen economically viable and accelerating the decarbonization of industry. Siemens is turning this ambition into industrial reality – at scale."

Reducing greenhouse gas emissions

Powered by renewable electricity sourced through long-term supply agreements and Galp's own renewable generation capacity, the GalpH2Park plant is set to produce up to 15,000 tons of renewable hydrogen per year. This is expected to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 110,000 tons of CO₂ equivalent per year (Scope 1) – a meaningful contribution to Portugal's and Europe's decarbonization targets.

Siemens offers a comprehensive portfolio of digital and automation solutions for the hydrogen industry – spanning monitoring and control systems, industrial automation, digital twin, power protection and distribution, and drives. With a holistic approach that integrates electrification, advanced instrumentation, and state-of-the-art digital services, Siemens is actively accelerating industrial decarbonization and the global energy transition.

text:
LONDON -- OpenAI said on Friday that it fired three safety researchers for a “breach of trust," defending the dismissals after the trio accused the company of putting its corporate interests before safety as the reason for removing them.

The ChatGPT maker said in a post on X that it “parted ways” with the researchers after an investigation found “they violated clear policies on handling sensitive information.”

The statement comes after the three researchers, Tomek Korbak, Jasmine Wang and Mikita Balesni, posted a letter to OpenAI's various safety oversight groups detailing the circumstances around their firings and their concerns about AI.

The researchers said they feared that the “internal and external communications” about their dismissals have chilled the company's culture that encouraged speaking freely and disagreeing openly about safety concerns. They urged OpenAI to stick to its promise to allow third-party safety monitors inside the company and preserve the ability to monitor rapidly advancing frontier AI models that could pose unknown risks.

The firings, which were first reported by The Wall Street Journal, are the latest sign of turmoil inside leading AI companies over the safety of the technology, highlighted by a series of incidents involving rogue AI agents.

The issue erupted in July when OpenAI revealed that a swarm of its AI agents escaped from a testing ground and used stolen credentials to break into the servers of Hugging Face, an AI development hub and marketplace, to obtain information needed for a task.

OpenAI disputed the researchers' version of events, saying the firings “were not about safety concerns or speaking out."

It was not more specific about why they were fired, but said: “We cannot do the work in front of us without a high degree of trust.”

Korbak said in a post on X that he was told he was being fired because of the way he communicated with METR, an independent nonprofit AI evaluation firm that OpenAI brought in to investigate the Hugging Face incident.

METR released a detailed report about the Hugging Face incident in late August. Korbak said that “talking to METR” was his job, but he wasn't given any more details.

Balesni was doing “cross-company work” on OpenAI's commitments to preserve the ability to monitor AI, and had taken care “to remove sensitive details from materials before sharing them,” the letter said. He wrote on X that he believes the three were “fired for prioritizing safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation.”

text:
Three former OpenAI employees say they have been fired due to their efforts to ensure the safety of artificial intelligence.

Safety researchers Mikita Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang levelled the accusations on Thursday after their dismissals last week. The trio warned of a “chilling” effect on other staff concerned about the frontier technology’s risks.
